welcome.hello.title: Welcome, Josephus
text: In 1725 the Viennese court composer Johann Joseph Fux published **Gradus ad Parnassum**, a course in composition written as a conversation between a master, Aloysius, and his pupil, Josephus. For two hundred years composers learned from it; Haydn is said to have worked through every exercise, and it is still used to teach today.
This game is that course. You play Josephus: Aloysius gives you a melody, you write a second melody against it, and the game judges your line by rules read from Fux's own pages.

You need **no musical knowledge** to start. This tutorial teaches you everything the game asks for: how to read a note, what an interval is, how two voices may move, and then each of Fux's five 'species', one after another, until you can write in three and four voices; and, last, the chords and figures that Bach's modes ask for. Every example you will hear is Fux's own.

welcome.goal.title: Where you are going
text: Here is what you will be writing by the end of the first-species chapter. Below: a plain, slow melody that never changes, the **cantus firmus**. Above: Fux's answer to it, one note against each of the cantus's notes.
Press ▶ under the score. Notice how the two lines are each singable on their own, and how together they never clash. That double demand is what 'counterpoint' means.
welcome.goal.prompt: Press ▶ to hear Fux's first example (Fig. 5 of the Gradus).
welcome.goal.done: That is the sound of first-species counterpoint. By the end of chapter 6 you will have written it yourself.

welcome.how.title: How the tutorial works
text: Each lesson is one short page: something to read, then something to do in the box below it — listen, answer a question, or write some notes. **Next** opens when the task is done.

Nothing here can be failed. If a writing task defeats you, **Hint** helps, and **Show me** writes Fux's answer for you; you can always **Skip** and come back. The contents at the side tick each lesson you finish, and the tutorial remembers where you stopped.
A word with a dotted line under it explains itself in the bar at the foot of the screen when you point at it. Turn your sound on, and let's begin.

notes.staff.title: The staff
text: Music is written on a **staff** of five lines. Each line, and each space between two lines, is one note: the higher on the staff, the higher the note sounds. Notes can go above or below the staff too, on short extra lines. Upright lines cut the staff into **bars**; here each bar holds one note.

Here there are two staves. The lower one holds a steady low note — ignore it for now. The upper one is yours. Click anywhere on it to write a note there; click again to replace it. Every note you write sounds, and its name appears beside it.
notes.staff.prompt: Write a note in each of the four bars, each one higher than the one before.
notes.staff.hint: Start near the bottom of the upper staff, then click a little higher in each bar.
notes.staff.done: You have written a rising line. Higher on the staff, higher in sound.

notes.letters.title: The seven letters
text: Notes are named with the first seven letters: **A B C D E F G**, and then A again, higher. Each line or space up the staff is the next letter. Moving to the very next letter, up or down, is a **step**.

The sign at the start of the upper staff is the **treble clef** (or G clef): its curl wraps round the line of G. The sign on the lower staff is the **bass clef** (or F clef): its two dots sit either side of the line of F. A clef tells you which letter each line is; the names beside the notes will spare you counting until you are used to it.
notes.letters.prompt: Write C, D, E and F, one in each bar, rising by step.
notes.letters.hint: Find a C (its name appears when you write it), then click one line or space higher for D, and so on.
notes.letters.done: C–D–E–F: four steps up the scale.

notes.octave.title: The octave
text: Climb eight letters from C and you reach C again: C D E F G A B C. The second C sounds like the first, only higher — so alike that we give it the same name. That distance is the **octave** (Latin for 'eighth').
The seven letters are the white keys of a piano. The black keys between them are the same letters raised or lowered a little; you will meet them in a moment.
notes.octave.prompt: Listen to the scale from C to C, and to two notes an octave apart.

clips.scale: C to C, step by step
clips.octave: C and the C above; D and the D above

notes.octave.done: Same letter, eight notes apart: the octave.

notes.steps.title: Steps and leaps
text: A melody moves either by **step** (to the next letter) or by **leap** (skipping at least one letter). Steps make a line smooth and singable; leaps give it shape. Fux's melodies move mostly by step, with an occasional leap, usually followed by a step back the other way.
Listen to G going straight to B, and to G going to B through A.
notes.steps.prompt: Is G up to B a step or a leap?

step.label: A step
step.why: Not quite: between G and B lies A. A step goes to the very next letter.

leap.label: A leap
leap.why: Yes: G to B skips the A between them. G–A–B would be two steps.

notes.steps.done: A leap over one letter is the smallest leap there is (a third, as you will see).

notes.sharp.title: Sharps and flats
text: A **sharp** (♯) raises a note by the smallest distance in this music, a **semitone** (on the piano, to the very next key, usually a black one). A **flat** (♭) lowers it by a semitone. A **natural** (♮) cancels either. Between most neighbouring letters lies a black key; between **E and F**, and between **B and C**, there is none: those steps are already semitones.

Fux writes almost only the seven plain letters. He adds a sharp or a flat for a reason, most often at the very end of a piece, where a voice rises a semitone into the last note: you will meet his C♯ before the final D again and again.
To write one: press ♯ below the staff, then click where the note goes. Or select a note you have written and press ♯ to raise it. ♭ and ♮ work the same way.
notes.sharp.prompt: Write a C♯ in either bar.
notes.sharp.hint: Write a C first (its name appears beside it), then press ♯ while it is selected.
notes.sharp.done: C♯: a semitone above C. You will need it at the end of almost every D-mode exercise.

intervals.count.title: Counting an interval
text: The distance between two notes is an **interval**. Count it in letters, **counting both ends**: from D to F is D, E, F — three letters — so it is a **third**. D to A (D E F G A) is a **fifth**. D to the D above is an **octave** (8). Two notes on the same pitch make a **unison** (1).
Larger intervals are named the same way and then thought of as their smaller form: D to the F above the next D is a **tenth**, which counts as a third. The note names are shown to help you count.
intervals.count.prompt: Count each interval, lower note to upper. Which number is it?
intervals.count.hint: Say the letters from the lower note up to the upper one, counting both, and wrap from G back to A.
intervals.count.done: You can measure any interval now. That is the counting the whole game rests on.

intervals.sound.title: Hearing intervals
text: Intervals do not all sound alike. Some sound **at rest**: the two notes melt together. Others **clash** and seem to want to move on. Fux's whole art is built on that difference.

Listen to each pair, played together. The third, the sixth, the fifth and the octave are restful. The second and the seventh rub. The fourth may surprise you: on its own it sounds quite open, yet in this style a fourth against the lowest voice is treated as a clash. The **tritone**, F against B, is 'mi against fa': the Gradus quotes the old verse mi contra fa est diabolus in musica, 'the devil in music'.
intervals.sound.done: Restful and restless: keep those two sounds in your ear.

intervals.classes.title: Perfect, imperfect, dissonant
text: Fux sorts intervals into three families:
**Perfect consonances**: the unison, the fifth and the octave. Completely stable — so stable that the rules limit how you may arrive at them.
**Imperfect consonances**: the third and the sixth (each comes in a major and a minor size). Sweet and restful, but not final. You may reach them freely, and Fux wants them often.

**Dissonances**: everything else — the second, the fourth, the seventh, and the tritone (F up to B) with its mirror, B up to F, which counts as a fifth but is not a perfect one. In the first species they are forbidden; later, each species allows them in carefully controlled ways.
A larger interval belongs to the family of its smaller form: a tenth is a third, a twelfth is a fifth.
intervals.classes.prompt: Which family does each interval belong to?
intervals.classes.hint: Count first. 1, 5, 8: perfect — except B up to F, which counts 5 but is the tritone. 3, 6: imperfect. 2, 4, 7: dissonant.
intervals.classes.done: Perfect, imperfect, dissonant: the three words you will use in every exercise.

motion.kinds.title: Four ways of moving
text: When two voices go from one pair of notes to the next, they move in one of four ways:

**Contrary**: one goes up, the other down. **Oblique**: one stays, the other moves. **Similar**: both go the same way, but by different distances. **Parallel**: both go the same way and keep the same interval (a third to a third, a fifth to a fifth).
Contrary motion keeps the voices independent, and Fux asks for it as much as possible (p. 45). Parallel motion makes them sound like one voice doubled.
motion.kinds.prompt: Listen to each kind of motion.

motion.quiz.title: Naming the motion
text: Each example is two pairs of notes, one after the other. Follow the lower voice, then the upper one: up, down or staying?
motion.quiz.prompt: Which kind of motion is it?
motion.quiz.hint: Both moving apart or together: contrary. One standing still: oblique. Both the same way: similar, or parallel if the interval stays the same.
motion.quiz.done: You can read motion now — and that is what the most important rule is about.

motion.rule.title: The great rule
text: Here it is, the rule Fux sets out before the first exercise: **reach a perfect consonance (unison, fifth, octave) only by contrary or oblique motion** — never by parallel or similar motion.
Listen to the two examples. Fifths in a row make the two voices fuse into one hollow, organ-like sound: the independence is lost. Reached from opposite directions, the same fifth sounds clean.
The upper voice starts on A, a fifth above the D. The lower voice then rises to E.
motion.rule.prompt: Write a note above the E in bar 2: any consonance, as long as you don't reach a fifth or an octave by parallel or similar motion.
motion.rule.hint: B would be a fifth reached in parallel — forbidden. Try G (a third) or C (a sixth).
motion.rule.done: That is the rule you will meet most often in the game.

cantus.firm.title: The cantus firmus
text: Every exercise starts from a **cantus firmus** ('fixed song'): a plain melody in long, equal notes, which never changes. Fux's are in the style of old church chant. Your task is always to write a second line against it.

This is the one Aloysius gives first. It begins and ends on D, moves mostly by step, and rises to a single high point. You will meet it in every chapter that follows: set five ways in two voices, and once more in three.
cantus.firm.prompt: Listen to the cantus firmus on D.
cantus.firm.done: D F E D G F A G F E D. Learn its shape: it is your companion for the rest of the tutorial.

cantus.modes.title: Modes and the final
text: Fux's melodies are not in major or minor keys but in **modes**: the scales you get by playing only the white keys of a piano, starting on different notes. Each mode is named by its **final**, the home note on which its melodies end. Fux uses six: on D, E, F, G, A and C.

Each has its own colour, because the semitones (E–F and B–C) fall in different places. The D mode has a darker colour, the C mode a brighter one — it is the 'major' scale of later music. The cantus firmus always begins and ends on the final, and so, at the very end, does your line.
cantus.modes.prompt: Listen to at least one of the modes (all six if you like).
cantus.modes.done: The game's exercises come in all six modes. The Lectio tab explains each one.

cantus.five.title: One melody, five species
text: Fux teaches counterpoint in five steps of rhythm, the **species**. Your line has: **1st** one note against each note of the cantus; **2nd** two notes; **3rd** four; **4th** notes held across the bar line (tied); **5th** all of these mixed, 'florid'.

The note lengths, with Fux's names in brackets: a **whole note** (semibreve) fills a bar; a **half note** (minim) half a bar; a **crotchet** (quarter note) a quarter; a **quaver** (eighth note) an eighth. A dot after a note makes it half as long again.
Each species adds one new freedom and one new rule for using it. Listen to Fux's answers, all five against the same cantus in D.
cantus.five.prompt: Listen to at least one of Fux's five answers.
cantus.five.done: Five rhythms, one melody underneath. Now you write them.

first.rules.title: Note against note
text: @quote:fux-mode.s1.01
In first species your line has one note against each note of the cantus. The intervals are shown between the staves. The rules:
1. **Every interval is a consonance** — no seconds, fourths, sevenths or tritones.
2. **A perfect consonance only by contrary or oblique motion** (the great rule).
3. **Begin on a perfect consonance**: unison, fifth or octave.
4. **End on the octave or the unison.**
5. **The cadence**: in the bar before the last, a **major sixth** when the cantus is below you. In D that means C♯ over the cantus's E, opening out to the octave D.
And two pieces of advice: prefer **imperfect** consonances (thirds and sixths) in the middle, and **contrary motion** wherever you can. Listen to Fux's line and read its intervals.

first.end.title: Write the ending
text: Fux's line is written out, except for the last two bars. The ending is fixed by the rules, so it is the best place to start. Aloysius gives the advice when the second species begins (p. 57), but it holds from the first: think of the end before you begin.

The last note must make an octave (or unison) with the cantus's final D. In the bar before, the cantus has E; you need the major sixth above it. E up to C is a minor sixth; E up to C♯, one semitone wider, is the major sixth. That C♯ is the **leading note**: a semitone below the final, it leads up into it.
first.end.hint: Bar 10: C♯ (write C, then ♯). Bar 11: the D just above it.
first.end.done: That is Fux's cadence in D: the sixth E–C♯ opening to the octave D–D.

first.begin.title: Write the beginning
text: Now the opening bar is empty. Begin on a **perfect consonance**: with your line above the cantus, the unison, the fifth or the octave above the D. Then listen to whether it leads well into Fux's second note.
first.begin.hint: Fux takes A, a fifth above D. The D an octave above works too.
first.begin.done: A perfect consonance to open, a perfect consonance to close: the frame of every first-species line.

first.middle.title: The middle of the line
text: Four bars in the middle are empty. Here you have the most freedom, and the coach under the score tells you, note by note, what each one makes against the cantus and how you reached it.
Aim for thirds and sixths, move against the cantus where you can, and keep your line singable: mostly steps, few leaps.
first.middle.hint: Fux: A, B, C, C. Over D, G, F, A that makes a fifth, a third, a fifth and a third.
first.middle.done: Every note consonant, every perfect consonance properly approached.

first.melody.title: A singable line
text: Aloysius also listens to your line as a melody, to be sung. As he raises them, these rules join the game (each exercise lists the ones in force under **How to play → Rules of this exercise**):
**No leap of a tritone** — F up to B, or B down to F: Fux's 'mi contra fa'. **No leap of a major sixth.**
**The unison** (both voices on the same note) **only in the first and the last bar** — and never leap into it or out of it.
**No leap into an octave with the voices closing in**: do not land on an octave or a unison by a leap while the two voices move towards each other.

Beyond the rules, keep leaps few and small, and follow a leap with a step the other way. Alfred Mann, in his English edition of the Gradus, advises no leap larger than a fifth, the octave and the rising minor sixth excepted.
first.melody.prompt: Which of these leaps may your line make?

tritone.label: F up to B
tritone.why: F–B is the tritone, three whole tones: forbidden as a leap.

sixth.label: C up to A
sixth.why: C–A is a major sixth: a leap the rules forbid.

fifth.label: D up to A
fifth.why: A fifth: the largest ordinary leap, and a good one.

first.melody.done: Mostly steps, a few small leaps: a line a singer can sing.

first.hint.title: The Hint button
text: In the game, a **Hint** button sits above the score (or press H). It looks at the place you are writing and tells you how many notes the rules allow there, given the rest of your line — and whether yours is one of them.

Ask it to **Suggest**, and it shows the note Fux would most likely write there, learnt from his other solutions (never from the one to this exercise). Use it when you are stuck, not to write the line for you: a line made of suggestions is not yet your own.
Hints work in two voices, species one to four; not yet in the fifth.

first.whole.title: A whole counterpoint
text: Now the staff is empty: write the whole line yourself. This is exactly the game's first exercise. Plan the ending first (C♯ then D), choose a perfect consonance to begin, and join them with consonances, moving against the cantus.
Your line does not have to be Fux's. Anything that keeps the rules is accepted — and in the game, once you have cleared one of Fux's worked exercises, his solution opens beside yours for comparison.
first.whole.hint: Ending: C♯, D. Beginning: A or D. In between, a third or a sixth above each cantus note keeps every rule; but for the gold 🌟 in the game, mix in contrary motion — a line that only moves in parallel with the cantus draws Aloysius's advice.
first.whole.done: Your first counterpoint. Aloysius would be pleased.

first.below.title: Writing below the cantus
text: @quote:fux-mode.s1.02

(Fux names his staves after the voices that sing them, alto and tenor; the game shows them in modern clefs.) He now puts the cantus in the upper voice and the counterpoint underneath. Two things change.
**The beginning**: below the cantus, begin on the octave or the unison, never the fifth. A fifth below D is G: your lowest note would put the piece in G, not in the mode of D.
**The cadence**: below the cantus, the bar before the last needs a **minor third**, C♯ under the E, closing to the unison D.
first.below.prompt: Write the first note and the last two.
first.below.hint: Bar 1: the D an octave below. Bar 10: C♯ just under the E. Bar 11: D, in unison with the cantus.
first.below.done: Above or below, the frame is the same: perfect at the ends, a semitone into the final.

first.game.title: Now in the game
text: The game has twelve first-species exercises: Fux's ten worked examples (modes on D, E, F, G and A, each with the cantus below and above), and two more on his C-mode cantus, which he leaves to private study. Rules join as Fux introduces them; each exercise lists its own under **How to play → Rules of this exercise**.

The cadence in every mode: the note before the last, in your line, is the note just below the final. In D it needs a sharp (C♯), in G too (F♯), and in A (G♯). In F and C it is a semitone already (E–F, B–C). In E your line comes from D, a whole tone below, because there the cantus itself falls the semitone F–E.

In the game you write on the full score, then press **Evaluate**. A result with no broken rule earns a ★, which opens the next exercise; with no piece of advice broken either, a gold 🌟. Clearing one of Fux's worked exercises also opens his own solution. You can come back to the tutorial any time with the TUTORIAL button.
first.game.prompt: Try the first exercise in the game, or carry on with the second species.

second.what.title: Two notes against one
text: @quote:fux-mode.s2.01
In second species your line has two half notes against each whole note of the cantus: the first on the **downbeat** (the strong half of the bar), the second on the **upbeat** (the weak half).

The new freedom: the upbeat note **may be dissonant**, if it is a **passing note** — reached by step and left by step in the same direction, filling in the gap of a third. The downbeat must still be consonant.
The line may open with a half rest. At the end: in the bar before the last, a fifth on the downbeat, then the major sixth (cantus below) on the upbeat.
On the score, a small 'A' or 'd' before a number means augmented or diminished: 'A4' is the augmented fourth, the tritone — not the note A.
second.what.prompt: Listen to Fux's second-species answer (Fig. 33). Watch the intervals on the upbeats.
second.what.done: The 4s on the upbeats (one of them the tritone, B over F) are passing notes: never on a downbeat, always by step.

second.passing.title: A passing note
text: In bar 5 the downbeat has B, a third above the cantus's G. The next bar begins on D. One note fits between B and D by step: write it on the upbeat. Against the G it makes a fourth — a dissonance, and exactly right here, because it passes.
second.passing.hint: B, ?, D: the letter between them.
second.passing.done: B–C–D: the C clashes with the G for a moment and moves straight on. That is a passing note.

second.bars.title: Two whole bars
text: Bars 6 and 7 are empty: four notes. Downbeats consonant; upbeats consonant, or dissonant only as passing notes. And read the downbeats on their own, as if the upbeats were not there: they must not make fifths or octaves in a row either.
second.bars.hint: Fux: D, A | C, D. Over F and A: a sixth, a third, a third, and a passing fourth.
second.bars.done: Downbeats that would work as first species, upbeats that join them.

second.cadence.title: The second-species cadence
text: In the bar before the last, Fux's second-species cadence is a fifth on the downbeat and the major sixth on the upbeat, which then opens to the octave. (In the E mode with the cantus above, that fifth would be B against F, a tritone, so Fux takes a sixth instead.)
second.cadence.prompt: Write the two notes of bar 10.
second.cadence.hint: Over the E: B (a fifth), then C♯ (the major sixth).
second.cadence.done: B–C♯–D: the fifth, the leading note, the octave.

second.game.title: Second species in the game
text: In the game, click the first half or the second half of a bar to write there. The **Rest** button puts the half rest at the start. There is one new rule that is easy to break by accident: never strike the same note twice in a row — two equal half notes are a whole note in disguise.
With the cantus above you, the cadence ends as in first species: the minor third under it (C♯ under E, in D), closing to the unison.
second.game.prompt: Try Fux's first second-species exercise, or go on to the third species.

third.what.title: Four notes against one
text: @quote:fux-mode.s3.01

Now four crotchets (quarter notes) against each whole note. The **first** crotchet of the bar must be consonant. The others may be dissonant when they **pass** by step in one direction — and in one more way, the **cambiata**, which you will write next.
With four notes a bar the line becomes a real melody: scales, turns, and leaps that open space. The cadence: the last crotchet before the final is the leading note, C♯ in D.
third.what.done: Many dissonances, all of them in passing: the downbeats keep the harmony.

third.cambiata.title: The cambiata
text: The **cambiata** ('exchanged note') is the one dissonance in this species that does not pass by step. The second crotchet steps down to a dissonance, the third **leaps down a third** to a consonance, and the fourth steps back up.
In bar 3 Fux writes E (an octave over the cantus's E), then D (a seventh: the dissonance), then — the empty place — then C.
third.cambiata.prompt: Write the third crotchet of bar 3, a third below the D.
third.cambiata.hint: From D, count three letters down: D, C, B.
third.cambiata.done: E–D–B–C: the cambiata. The dissonant D leaps away instead of resolving by step.

third.bar.title: A bar of crotchets
text: Bar 5 is empty. Bar 4 ends on A; bar 6 begins on F, high up. Climb from one to the other by step, one note for each crotchet. Check the first crotchet: it must be consonant against the cantus's G.
third.bar.prompt: Write the four crotchets of bar 5.
third.bar.hint: From A up to F: B (or B♭, as Fux writes), C, D, E.
third.bar.done: A scale between two consonances: the crotchets in between may clash, because they pass.

third.cadence.title: The third-species cadence
text: The bar before the last, against the cantus's E. Climb to the leading note: the fourth crotchet must be the major sixth, C♯, which rises into the final D.
third.cadence.prompt: Write the four crotchets of bar 10.
third.cadence.hint: G, A, B, C♯ — up by step.
third.cadence.done: G–A–B–C♯–D: the line runs up into the final.

third.game.title: Third species in the game
text: In the game the keyboard is fastest for crotchets: type the letters (A to G) and each note is written and the selection moves on; ↑ ↓ correct the note just written. Clicking works too. As in second species, never strike the same note twice in a row.
With the cantus above you, the last crotchet before the final is the minor third under the cantus (C♯ under E, in D).
third.game.prompt: Try Fux's first third-species exercise, or go on to the fourth species.

fourth.what.title: Notes tied across the bar
text: @quote:fux-mode.s4.01

(Fux's **arsis** is the upbeat, his **thesis** the downbeat.) In fourth species your line moves on the **upbeat** and is **tied** over the bar line, so it is held while the cantus changes underneath. A **tie** is the curved line joining two notes of the same pitch: they sound as one long note.

That held note is the **ligature**. When the cantus moves under it, it may become a dissonance — a **suspension**. It must then **resolve by step down** to a consonance on the upbeat. The note it is tied from (the **preparation**) must be consonant.
Preparation (consonant) → suspension (may clash) → resolution (a step down, consonant): listen for the 7 resolving to 6 again and again.
fourth.what.done: Tension and release, bar after bar: the suspension is the soul of this species.

fourth.resolve.title: Resolve the suspension
text: In bar 3 the D is tied over from bar 2. Against the cantus's E it is now a seventh: a suspension. It must resolve a step down, on the upbeat, to a consonance.
fourth.resolve.done: D over E (a seventh) falls to C (a sixth): the 7–6 suspension.

fourth.chain.title: A chain of suspensions
text: Fux likes the 7–6 in chains: each resolution is itself tied over and, when the cantus moves, may become the next suspension. Bar 3 ends on C. Tie it into bar 4 (write C again on the downbeat — the game draws the tie), let it resolve down a step, then tie that note into bar 5.
fourth.chain.prompt: Write the downbeat and upbeat of bar 4, and the downbeat of bar 5.
fourth.chain.hint: C (tied), B♭ (press ♭ before writing B), B♭ (tied). Fux uses B♭ here; B♮ also fits the rules.
fourth.chain.done: C over D (a seventh) falls to B♭ (a sixth), which is held into the next bar: a chain.

fourth.cadence.title: The fourth-species cadence
text: At the end, the leading note arrives as the resolution of a suspension: D is tied over the E as a seventh, and resolves down to C♯, the major sixth, which rises into the final.
fourth.cadence.prompt: Write the downbeat and upbeat of bar 10.
fourth.cadence.done: The 7–6 cadence: the most Fux-like ending of all.

fourth.game.title: Fourth species in the game
text: In the game, write the same note again on the downbeat to tie it; the **Tie** button (or T) repeats the previous note for you. Aloysius wants a ligature wherever one is possible; plain half notes only where none fits.

The upbeat is always a new note: never strike the downbeat's note again in the same bar. With the cantus above, your suspensions lie under it: a second resolving to a third (2–3), or a fourth to a fifth (4–5) — never 7–8; and the cadence is a second tied over, resolving to the minor third.
fourth.game.prompt: Try Fux's first fourth-species exercise, or go on to the fifth species.

fifth.what.title: Florid counterpoint
text: @quote:fux-mode.s5.01

The fifth species mixes everything: half notes, crotchets, ties and a few **quavers** (eighth notes), each value treated as in its own species. Dissonances pass, form cambiatas, or are suspended and resolved.

Two new points of style: quavers come only in pairs, on the second or fourth crotchet of the bar, never on the first or third; and a dissonance may never simply be struck on a downbeat — only tied into it.
fifth.what.done: A garden of figures: all four earlier species in one line.

fifth.choose.title: Which bar is florid and correct?
text: Here are three versions of bar 3, against the cantus's E. Each option shows the line around it; listen and look. Only one keeps the rules of the fifth species.
fifth.choose.prompt: Choose the bar that keeps the rules.

quavers.label: G F E — quavers first
quavers.why: Two quavers on the first crotchet of the bar: quavers belong on the second or fourth crotchet.

fux.label: G, F, E, G in crotchets
fux.why: Fux's own bar: G is consonant on the downbeat, F passes between G and E, E and G are consonant.

struck.label: F, then G, in half notes
struck.why: F against E is a second, struck on the downbeat: a dissonance on the downbeat must be tied over and resolved, never struck.

fifth.choose.done: Every value keeps the rule of its own species.

fifth.game.title: Fifth species in the game
text: In the game, first choose the **value** of the next note with the note buttons (or the keys 8 4 3 2 6 1: quaver, crotchet, dotted crotchet, minim, dotted minim, whole bar), then click or type the letter. **Hold** (T) continues the note before, over the bar line as a tie. There are twelve exercises, all Fux's.

Three more points the game checks: tie over the bar line only from the second half of a bar; vary the values (a line of half notes is not florid); and two crotchets opening a bar want a tied note, or two more crotchets, after them.
fifth.game.prompt: Try Fux's first fifth-species exercise, or go on to three voices.

three.bass.title: Three voices: the bass
text: In three voices the cantus is joined by two lines of yours. Here the cantus in D is on top, and Fux's two voices are below it (Fig. 101).

Everything is now measured from the **bass**: the lowest note sounding in each bar, whichever voice it belongs to. Every voice must be consonant **against the bass**. Between the two upper voices a fourth is allowed — but not a second or a seventh.

The numbers under the upper notes are their intervals above the bass. Here, in first species, every voice sings whole notes; the game has the other four species in three voices too, where one of your voices moves while the other holds whole notes.
three.bass.done: Three voices, one harmony in each bar.

three.chords.title: The full triad
text: Aloysius (p. 82): in every setting, 'unless some other reason prevents it, the harmonic triad is to be used' — a **third and a fifth above the bass** (figured 5/3). A sixth may take the fifth's place, for the line's sake: a third and a sixth (6/3, the **six-three**). An octave may stand in for the fifth too, to avoid perfect consonances in a row. A bar of only perfect consonances sounds bare; the game notes it as advice. The first and last bars are free.
Look at the figures of the highlighted bar.
three.chords.prompt: What stands above the bass in this bar?
three.chords.hint: Find the lowest note; count up to each of the other two (larger intervals reduced: 10 is 3).

choices.incomplete: Incomplete — no fifth or sixth above the bass

three.chords.done: Full triads in the middle; at the ends an incomplete sound (D–F–D to open, octaves to close).

three.fill.title: Fill the middle voice
text: Bars 5 and 6 of the middle voice are empty. In bar 5 the bass has E and the cantus G: the triad wants the fifth above the bass. In bar 6 the bass has D and the cantus F. Avoid fifths and octaves in a row between any two voices — not only against the bass.
three.fill.prompt: Write the middle voice in bars 5 and 6.
three.fill.hint: Bar 5: B, the fifth above E. Bar 6: not A, the fifth — after B over E that would make fifths in a row with the bass. Fux takes D, an octave above the bass.
three.fill.done: Fux's middle voice. Writing for two voices at once means checking three pairs.

three.cadence.title: The three-voice cadence
text: In the bar before the last, both your voices are empty. The bass must arrive on the final, D; one voice must reach it by a semitone (here C♯ rising; in the E mode, F falling). The cantus sings E above.
three.cadence.prompt: Write the middle voice and the bass of bar 10.
three.cadence.hint: Bass: A (it falls a fifth to the final D). Middle voice: C♯ (it rises a semitone to D).
three.cadence.done: A, C♯, E: a full triad, every voice moving to its place in the final chord.

three.moving.title: Three voices, one moving
text: After first species, Fux takes three voices through the other four species too (Exercitium II, Lectiones II–V, 1725, pp. 94–114). One of your voices takes the new rhythm — minims, crotchets, ligatures, or florid — while the other keeps to whole notes with the cantus.

What you know carries over: the moving voice keeps the rules of its species, and on each downbeat the three voices make the harmony of the first three-voice lesson. Fux also grants a little more freedom; for instance, two fifths or octaves on successive downbeats are saved by a leap of a third in between (p. 94), where two voices needed a fourth.
Listen to his first example of each: again the same cantus in D, now with two companions.
three.moving.prompt: Listen to at least one of Fux's examples.
three.moving.done: One cantus, two companions, one of them dancing.

three.game.title: Three voices in the game
text: Choose **3 voices** in the first menu. You write both voices that are not the cantus, in any order: clicking a staff writes there and makes it the active voice; with the keyboard, **V** switches between your two voices. All five species are there, Fux's exercises in his order: in species two to five one of your voices takes the new rhythm while the other keeps to whole notes. The two-voice rules of each species hold for the moving voice, and the three-voice rules for the harmony on the downbeats.

What the game checks besides: begin and end with the final as the lowest note; in the last bar the other voices take its octave, its fifth or its major third — never the minor third (in D, no F♮ over the final D); and in your voices no tritone, major sixth or seventh leaps.
three.game.prompt: Try Fux's first three-voice exercise, or read ahead about four voices.

four.preview.title: Four voices
text: The Gradus ends its course in four voices (Exercitium III), and so does the game: choose **4 voices** in the first menu. Against the cantus you write three voices, species by species: Fux's own exercises first, then the modes he leaves to private study, without a solution of his, and last the species combined, each voice in its own rhythm.

What changes is mostly arithmetic. A triad has three different notes, so with four voices one of them must be **doubled**, sung by two voices at once. Fux says which: the octave of the bass first; where that would give faulty progressions, the third, more rarely the sixth (p. 114). The voices also share the space: from high to low, soprano, alto, tenor, bass, each kept singable and, Fux adds, the closer together the fuller the harmony.

And the more voices, the harder it is to avoid every hidden fifth and octave: Fux tolerates them where necessity forces them (p. 115), and so the game notes them as advice, not as faults. In species two to five one voice moves and two hold semibreves, which in the fourth and fifth species may be divided into two minims where a clash would otherwise be unavoidable (pp. 132–133).

fugue.what.title: What a fugue is
text: Everything you have learnt leads here. A **fugue** is counterpoint grown into a whole piece: several voices, each a real melody, all built from one short theme, the **subject**.

Johann Sebastian Bach wrote the most famous collection of them, **The Well-Tempered Clavier**: two books (the first finished in 1722, the second some twenty years later), each with a prelude and a fugue in every major and minor key — 48 in all, all of them in the game's study.

Here is the first fugue of Book I, in C major. Listen to the subject alone: a rising scale, a little turn, a leap, and a run down. Then hear how the piece begins: one voice alone sings it, and a second joins.
fugue.what.prompt: Listen to the subject, then to the opening.
fugue.what.done: Remember the subject's shape: you will now follow it through the piece.

fugue.entries.title: The entries
text: A fugue opens with its **exposition**: the voices come in one by one, each with the subject (or its answer), until all are singing. Each time the subject begins in a voice is an **entry**.
When a voice has sung the subject it does not stop: it goes on in counterpoint against the next entry — exactly the art you practised with Fux, now against a moving theme instead of a cantus firmus.
Listen to each entry of the exposition on its own, voice by voice.
fugue.entries.prompt: Listen to every entry of the exposition.
fugue.entries.done: Same tune, different heights: each voice in its own register.

fugue.voices.title: How many voices?
text: Now the whole exposition, every voice together. Count the entries as they come in: each one is a new voice joining.
fugue.voices.prompt: How many voices does this fugue have?

v3.label: Three
v3.why: Listen again: after the third entry, one more voice comes in, low down.

v4.label: Four
v4.why: Four voices: once all four have entered, the exposition is over.

v5.label: Five
v5.why: Not so many: count the entries of the subject — four, one in each voice.

fugue.voices.done: Four voices — like a choir of soprano, alto, tenor and bass.

fugue.answer.title: Subject and answer
text: The second voice does not sing the subject at the same pitch: it sings it **a fifth higher**. This entry is called the **answer**. The pattern — subject in the home key, answer a fifth above — is the backbone of every exposition.
Sometimes the answer has to change a note or two to stay in the key (a **tonal** answer, as against a **real** one); the study's exercises let you decide which, fugue by fugue.
Listen to the subject, then to the answer, then to the two together as Bach writes them.

clips.answerAlone: The answer (a fifth higher, on G)

fugue.answer.done: Subject and answer: the call and the reply.

fugue.stretto.title: Stretto
text: After the exposition, the subject keeps returning, in different voices and on different notes; between returns there may be passages built from its fragments (**episodes**).

Sometimes a voice starts the subject **before the previous entry has finished**, so that the entries overlap like a round. This is a **stretto** ('tightened'), and this fugue is full of them: by the study's count the subject enters 23 times in 27 bars.
Listen to two overlapping entries alone, then with everything around them.
fugue.stretto.prompt: Listen to the stretto, alone and in context.
fugue.stretto.done: The subject chasing itself: the densest counterpoint of all.

fugue.study.title: The Well-Tempered Clavier study
text: The game's **Well-Tempered Clavier** mode lets you go as deep as you like into all 48 preludes and fugues:
• a **roll** that shows every voice in its own colour, with each entry of the subject outlined (and upside down where Bach inverts it); click an entry to hear it;
• a **spotlight** that plays one voice in another sound, so you can follow it through the texture;
• a **page** of score that follows the music as it plays;
• a **harmony** reading, the piece's keys, and the **temperament** (the old tunings that gave the collection its name);
• a **workshop**: change the subject's notes and hear the whole fugue sung with your version, or add entries of your own.
It opens on the fugue you have just heard.

harmony.triad.title: The triad
text: Fux's counterpoint is built note by note, but its sonorities are already chords: the 'harmonic triad' Aloysius asks for in three voices is a **third and a fifth above the bass**. Take any note, add the note a third above it and the note a third above that: a **triad**. Its lowest note in that stack is the **root**; the others are its **third** and its **fifth**.

The third decides its colour. A **major** triad has a major third (four semitones) under a perfect fifth; a **minor** triad a minor third (three semitones) under a perfect fifth; a **diminished** triad a minor third under a diminished fifth, the tense one.
harmony.triad.done: Major, minor, diminished: the three triads that a major scale makes from its own notes.

harmony.degrees.title: Degrees: the Roman numerals
text: Build a triad on each note of the C major scale, using only the scale's notes, and you get seven chords. They are named by the **degree** of their root, counted from the key note (the **tonic**) in Roman numerals: I on C, II on D, and so on to VII on B.

Upper case for a major triad, lower case for a minor one, a small circle for the diminished: in any major key **I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°**. The three major ones carry the key: **I** the tonic, **V** the dominant, **IV** the subdominant.
harmony.degrees.prompt: Listen to the triads of C major, I to the octave.

clips.scale: I ii iii IV V vi vii° I

harmony.degrees.done: Those numerals are the ones the Chorales mode asks for, and the ones the study writes above the music.

harmony.degreesQuiz.title: Name the degree
text: Find the root (the note with the others a third and a fifth above it), count from C to it, and choose upper or lower case by the third.
harmony.degreesQuiz.prompt: In C major: which degree is this chord?
harmony.degreesQuiz.hint: Root on C is I, on D ii, on E iii, on F IV, on G V, on A vi, on B vii°.

harmony.minor.title: Minor keys
text: In a minor key the numerals change case: in A minor the tonic chord is **i** (A–C–E), the subdominant **iv** (D–F–A), and **VI** (F–A–C) and **III** (C–E–G) are major.

The dominant is the exception. A minor's own seventh note is G, which gives a minor v (E–G–B); but to lead into the tonic the seventh is raised a semitone, **G♯**, and the dominant becomes major: **V** (E–G♯–B). It is the same semitone Fux demands at every close, the raised seventh rising to the final.
harmony.minor.prompt: Listen to i, iv, V, VI, V, i in A minor; hear the G♯ pull towards A.

clips.minor: i iv V VI V i

harmony.minor.done: Major V, minor tonic: the sound of a minor key.

harmony.figures.title: Inversions and figures
text: A triad need not stand on its root. Whatever note is lowest is the **bass**, and the chord is named by the intervals above it, the **figures** that Baroque players read under a bass line (the 'thoroughbass').

Root in the bass: a third and a fifth above it, **5/3** (root position). Third in the bass: a third and a sixth, **6/3**, written simply 6 (first inversion; Fux's six-three). Fifth in the bass: a fourth and a sixth, **6/4** (second inversion), unstable, used mostly on the way to a cadence. The same chord, three basses.
harmony.figures.prompt: Listen to C–E–G over C, over E, over G, and read the figures under the bass staff.
harmony.figures.done: Figures count from the bass, whatever the root.

harmony.figuresQuiz.title: Read the figures
text: Find the lowest note, then count up to each of the others (an octave and more reduced): 3 and 5, 3 and 6, or 4 and 6.
harmony.figuresQuiz.prompt: Which figures stand over the bass?
harmony.figuresQuiz.hint: A fourth above the bass means 6/4; a sixth with a third means 6/3.
harmony.figuresQuiz.done: Root position, first inversion, second inversion.

harmony.sevenths.title: Seventh chords
text: Add one more third above the fifth and the triad becomes a **seventh chord**: on G, G–B–D–F, the **dominant seventh** (V7), whose F wants to fall to E and whose B wants to rise to C.

With four notes there are four basses, and four sets of figures, each named by its most telling intervals: root in the bass **7**; third in the bass **6/5**; fifth in the bass **4/3**; seventh in the bass **4/2** (written 2, and in full 6/4/2, as the Preludes mode prints it).
Under the bass staff the game lists every interval above the bass (6, d5, 3 for the second chord); the figure names only the telling ones (6/5), the rest being understood.
harmony.sevenths.prompt: Listen to G–B–D–F over each of its notes.
harmony.sevenths.done: The seventh in the bass, 4/2, must fall a step: Bach's preludes are full of it.

harmony.seventhsQuiz.title: Seventh chords by their figures
text: Find the bass, then look for the second (two neighbouring letters) inside the chord: where it lies decides the figures.
harmony.seventhsQuiz.hint: A second right above the bass: 4/2. A second at the top of a third: 4/3. A fifth and a sixth over the bass: 6/5. Bass, third, fifth, seventh stacked: 7.

harmony.cadences.title: Cadences
text: A phrase ends on a **cadence**: two chords that close it. The four kinds have names (later ones than Fux's):
• **authentic**: V to I, the full close (Fux's clausula, the raised seventh rising to the final, sounds inside it);
• **half**: a phrase that stops on V, a comma rather than a full stop;
• **plagal**: IV to I, the 'Amen';
• **deceptive**: V that goes, not to I, but to vi.
harmony.cadences.prompt: Listen to the four, in C.
harmony.cadences.done: Where a chorale's phrases end, and on which of these chords, is the first level of the Chorales mode.

harmony.cadenceQuiz.title: Name the cadence
text: Name the two chords as degrees of the key, then the cadence: V–I, IV–I, V–vi, or a phrase ending on V.
harmony.cadenceQuiz.hint: Find the root of each chord and count from the tonic.
harmony.cadenceQuiz.done: That is the harmony the chorales and preludes ask for.

harmony.modes.title: Harmony in the game
text: Three places in the game use what this chapter taught. **Chorales**: at each fermata of a chorale melody, choose the chord the phrase cadences on (I, V, vi …), then compare with Kittel's basses and Bach's own settings. **WTC · preludes and harmony**: over Bach's bass in the C major prelude, choose each bar's chord by its figures (5/3, 6/3, 6/4/2 …) and compare with Bach's plan. **The Well-Tempered Clavier** study writes the Roman numerals of the chords above the music.
Neither mode marks anything wrong: Bach's choices are the comparison.

end.path.title: The road to the end
text: This is the whole game, in order: two voices, then three, then four, each through the five species. Each exercise cleared earns a ★, and a gold 🌟 if no advice was broken either; the menus count them for each species. Clearing one of Fux's worked exercises also opens his own solution, to see, hear and compare with yours. Some exercises (the C cantus in first species; the G, A and C cantus in third and fourth) are ones he left to private study: there is no solution of his to compare.

When an exercise defeats you: open **How to play → Rules of this exercise** for the rules in force, read the **Lectio** for what Fux says about it, and look at the marks after **Evaluate** — each tells you which bar breaks which rule and why. Then come back here: every species has its chapter.

Beyond Fux lie Bach's modes: the **Well-Tempered Clavier** (listening and fugue exercises; the tutorial's fugue chapter prepares it), and the **Chorales** and **WTC · preludes and harmony**, which ask for the chords and figures of the harmony chapter.

end.tour.title: A tour of the game screen
text: Last, the screen itself. The tour opens the game on your two-voice exercise and points at each part in turn: where to choose an exercise, where to write, how to listen, how to be judged, and where the rules and Fux's text live.
You can leave the tour at any moment, and start it again from here.

say.notHigher: Bar {bar} is not higher than the bar before it.
say.notStep: Bar {bar} is not the very next note up: click one line or space above the note before.
say.sharpNow: Now select the C and press ♯ (or press ♯ first, then write the C).
say.sharpOther: That is a sharp, but not on a C.

coach.perfect: Bar {bar}: {note} against {cf} — a {interval}, a perfect consonance.
coach.imperfect: Bar {bar}: {note} against {cf} — a {interval}, an imperfect consonance.
coach.dissonantFirst: Bar {bar}: {note} against {cf} — a {interval}: a dissonance, not allowed in first species.
coach.dissonantDown: Bar {bar}: {note} against {cf} — a {interval}: a dissonance on the downbeat, not allowed here.
coach.dissonantTied: Bar {bar}: {note} against {cf} — a {interval}: a dissonance; on the downbeat it must be tied over and resolve a step down.
coach.dissonantWeak: Bar {bar}: {note} against {cf} — a {interval}: a dissonance; fine only if it passes by step (or forms a cambiata).
coach.motionBad.parallel: Reached by parallel motion: a perfect consonance in parallel — forbidden.
coach.motionBad.similar: Reached by similar motion: a perfect consonance reached that way is forbidden.
coach.tritoneLeap: The leap into it is a tritone (augmented fourth): forbidden.
coach.majorSixthLeap: The leap into it is a major sixth: forbidden.
coach.seventhLeap: The leap into it is a seventh: hard to sing, and forbidden outright in three voices.

quiz.figure: Which figures stand over the bass?
quiz.why.figure: {bass} is in the bass, the chord's {member} (its root is {root}).

intro.title: The game screen
intro.text: This is the game screen, on the two-voice exercise you were last at: the cantus firmus and your staff. Let's walk round it.

nav.title: Choosing an exercise
nav.text: Three menus: the number of voices, the species, and the exercise (its number, the final of its mode, and whether the cantus is below or above). ‹ › step through the exercises in order. A ★ marks each one you have cleared.

score.title: The score
score.text: Your staff and the cantus. Click or tap your staff to write; drag a note to move it. Pinch, Ctrl + wheel, or − / + above the score change the size.

view.title: View
view.text: Turn on the note names (letters or do-re-mi) and the intervals between the staves — the training wheels you used in the tutorial.

hint.title: Hint
hint.text: Stuck on a note? Hint (or H) tells how many notes the rules allow where you are writing and whether yours is one; Suggest shows the most Fux-like.

write.title: Writing
write.text: ♭ ♮ ♯ for accidentals, the Rest, Tie, Hold and note-value buttons where the species needs them, Clear all, and undo / redo.

evaluate.title: Evaluate
evaluate.text: When every place is filled, press Evaluate (the number on it counts the empty places). Aloysius marks each broken rule on the score, and a line under the transport sums up.

listen.title: Listening
listen.text: ▶ plays your line with the cantus; ▶| from the selected bar (Space); ⟲ loops; the faders set tempo and volume.

star.title: The star
star.text: No rule broken earns the ★ (and opens the next exercise when the game is not in BETA); no advice broken either, the gold 🌟. Clearing the exercise also opens Fux's own solution.

fux.title: Fux's solution
fux.text: Once you have cleared an exercise, ◇ Fux shows his line beside yours on the score; the Evaluation tab compares the two, with his reasons.

dock.title: The tabs
dock.text: Mixer: the sounds, drums and a basso continuo, for pleasure. Evaluation: the details of the judgement. How to play: the controls, the basics and the rules of this exercise. Lectio: Fux's own text for this exercise, with a translation.

info.title: The info bar
info.text: Point at anything — a button, a dotted word — and this bar explains it. On a phone, tap ⓘ first.

help.title: Help and the tutorial
help.text: HOW TO PLAY opens the guide; TUTORIAL brings you back here. That's the whole screen: good luck, Josephus.
